Ibn Juzayy's commentary on surah 45, verse 9:

﴿And when he learns something of Our verses﴾: meaning, when some part of them reaches him, and he does not intend true knowledge.
"From behind them is Hell" (min wara'ihim jahannam), like His saying: "And before him is a severe punishment" (wa-min wara'ihi 'adhabun ghalizun). It has been mentioned in Ibrahim [14:17].

ۡ**﴿And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾**: meaning the sun, the moon, the angels, the children of Adam, the animals, the plants, and other things. **﴿all of it from Him﴾**: that is, every blessing is from Allah, the Exalted. The prepositional phrase (majrur, "from Him") is either in a position of circumstance (hal) or is the predicate of an implied subject (khabar mubtada' mudmar). Ibn 'Abbas recited it as **مِنَّةً** (minnatan, "as a favor").

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 45, verse 14:

﴿Say to those who believe: forgive those who do not expect the Days of Allah﴾ Allah commanded the believers to overlook the disbelievers and not to hold them to account when they harmed them, and this was at the beginning of Islam. It is said that it has been abrogated (mansukhah) by the sword (al-naskh, abrogation), and it is said that it has not been abrogated, because bearing harm is recommended in every case, whereas fighting for Islam is not included in that. It is narrated that the verse was revealed concerning ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him): a man among the disbelievers insulted him, and ʿUmar wished to seize him. "The Days of Allah" are His blessings, so "expect" (al-rajaʾ) retains its original meaning. It is also said that "the Days of Allah" refers to His punishment, so al-rajaʾ here means fear. "Yaghfiru" (let them forgive) is in the jussive mood as the answer to an implied condition indicated by "qul" (say). Al-Zamakhshari said: the object of the verb "qul" has been omitted, and the meaning is: "Say to them, 'Forgive,' they will forgive." ﴿That He may recompense a people for what they used to earn﴾: the subject of "yajziya" (He may recompense) is a pronoun referring to Allah, and it has been read with the first-person plural nun (nunation of the speaker). Ibn ʿAtiyya said that the verse is a threat, so "qawm" (a people) here means those who do not expect the Days of Allah, and "yaksibun" (they earn) means their evil deeds. Al-Zamakhshari said: "qawm" are those who believe, and their recompense is reward for what they used to earn, by restraining anger and bearing what is disliked.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 45, verse 21:

﴿Do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe?﴾ Am (أم) here is for denial (إنكار). Ijtarahu (اجترحوا) means they acquired (اكتسبوا). The intended meaning of ﴿those who commit evil deeds﴾ is the disbelievers, because they are contrasted with "those who believe," and because the verse is Meccan. Its wording may also include believing sinners, and for this reason it is related that al-Fudayl ibn Iyad recited it at night and kept repeating it and weeping throughout the night, saying to himself: "To which of the two groups do you belong?" Its meaning is a denial of what the disbelievers supposed, that they and the believers would be equal in life and in death. In its interpretation there are two opinions. The first is that the intended meaning is that the believers are not equal to the disbelievers, neither in life nor in death, for the believers lived in piety and obedience, while the disbelievers lived in disbelief and disobedience, and so their communities are not equal. The second opinion is that they are equal in life in worldly matters, such as health and provision, but they are not equal in death; rather the believers are made happy and the disbelievers are made wretched. Thus the intended meaning is the affirmation of recompense in the Hereafter and the preference of the believers over the disbelievers in the Hereafter. This meaning is the more apparent and the more preponderant, and the sense of the verse is like His saying: ﴿Shall We treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ [al-Qalam: 35], and ﴿Or shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on earth? Or shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28]. ﴿Their living and their dying are alike﴾: this clause is a substitute (بدل) for the kaf (الكاف) in His saying ﴿like those who believe﴾, and it explains the comparison (مفسرة للتشبيه). It falls within what Allah denied of what the disbelievers supposed. It was also said that it is an independent (مستأنف) statement; the meaning according to this is that the living and dying of the believers are alike, and the living and dying of the disbelievers are alike, because each one dies upon what he lived upon. This meaning is remote, and the correct view is that it is a complement of what precedes it according to the meaning we have chosen. As for its grammatical analysis (إعراب): whoever reads sawa'un (سواء) with a raised vowel (بالرفع) takes it as the subject (مبتدأ) with its predicate being mahyahum and mamatuhum, and the clause is a substitute for the prepositional phrase that serves as the second object of naj'al. Whoever reads sawa'an (سواءً) with a fatha (بالنصب) takes it as a circumstantial accusative (حال) or as the second object of naj'al, and mahyahum is the agent (فاعل) of sawa', since it carries the meaning of mustawin (مستوى). ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾: that is, evil is their judgment in placing themselves on a par with the believers.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary on Surah 45 (al-Jathiyah), verse 22:

﴿And that every soul may be recompensed for what it has earned﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with His saying "with truth," because it carries the sense of causation (ta'lil). Or it is coordinated with a deleted causal clause whose implied meaning is: God created the heavens and the earth to show by them His power, and so that every soul may be recompensed for what it has earned.

**﴿Has taken his own desire as his god﴾**: that is, he obeys it until it becomes to him like a deity. **﴿And Allah has led him astray knowingly﴾**: that is, with a prior knowledge from Allah. It was also said: it means with knowledge on the part of this misguided person that he is in error, yet he follows error out of obstinacy. **﴿And He has sealed﴾**: this was mentioned in al-Baqarah [7]. **﴿Who then can guide him after Allah?﴾** Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: there is an omitted genitive here, its estimated meaning being "after Allah's leading him astray." It may also mean: "who can guide him other than Allah?"

**﴿And they said﴾**: the pronoun refers either to those who have taken their own desire as their god, or to the Quraysh. **﴿We die and we live﴾**: there are four interpretations of this. The first is that they meant: some people die and others live. The second is: we die and our children live. The third is: we die when we were nonexistent or drops of sperm, and we live in this world. The fourth is: we die the known death, and we live before it in this world; so there is a transposition in the wording. Their intended meaning in every case is a denial of the Hereafter. It appears that they held the doctrine of the Dahriyyah (those who attribute everything to time and deny the Hereafter), as shown by their saying: **﴿Nothing destroys us but time﴾**. Allah refuted them with His words: **﴿And they have no knowledge of that﴾**, to the end of the verse.

**﴿They said: Bring back our fathers﴾**: this was mentioned in al-Dukhan [36]. **﴿Say: Allah gives you life﴾**, to the end of the verse: this is a refutation of those who deny the resurrection (hashr, the gathering of people for judgment), and an argument for its occurrence from Allah's power to give life and cause death.

And you will see every nation kneeling (jathiyah), (meaning) falling to their knees, and that is the posture of one who is fearful and humbled. Every nation will be called to its record (kitab) today, (meaning) to the scrolls of their deeds. It was also said that the kitab here is the book revealed to them. The first view is more likely (arjah) because of His saying: ﴿This Our Record speaks against you with truth﴾ (the verse). If it is asked: how does He attribute the Book (kitab) at one time to them and at another time to Allah, Exalted is He? The answer: He attributed it to them because their deeds are recorded in it, and He attributed it to Allah, Exalted is He, because He is its Owner, and it is He who commanded the angels to write it. ﴿Indeed, We used to have it copied down what you used to do﴾. That is, We commanded the angels who guard you to write down your deeds. It was also said that Allah commands the guardians (hafazah) to copy (tanskh) the deeds of the servants from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), and then they keep it with them, so the deeds of the servants come in accordance with that, and the angels record them; that is the istinsakh (copying). Ibn 'Abbas used to argue for this by saying: "Copying (istinsakh) is only done from an original (asl)."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 45, verse 34:

﴿Today We forsake you, as you forgot the meeting of this your Day﴾. The forgetting here means abandonment (al-tark). As for His words ﴿as you forgot﴾, it may mean either abandonment (al-tark) or heedlessness (al-dhuhul).
﴿Nor will they be allowed to seek to make amends﴾ (yustaʿtabūn), from al-ʿUtbā, which means contentment (al-ridā).
